paragraphs.title: Summoning the Divine Army Against Babylon

easy.q: Against which city is the burden in this passage directed?

easy.explanation: Verse 2 says, “Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain.”
easy.q: What were the people commanded to lift up on the high mountain?

easy.explanation: Verse 4 declares, “The Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle.”
easy.q: Who musters the host of the battle?

answers: They serve as instruments of the Lord’s indignation
They come to trade with Babylon
medium.explanation: Verse 5 connects them with “the weapons of his indignation” to destroy the land.
medium.q: What role do the peoples coming from distant lands serve in the passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase introduces Isaiah’s prophetic message concerning Babylon.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “the burden of Babylon” introduce?

answers: The nations flee, and then the banner is lifted
Babylon is rebuilt, and then shepherds arrive
A banner is lifted, mighty ones are called, and the nations gather
medium.explanation: The passage moves from the raised banner and summoned warriors to the gathering of nations.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the summons to battle?

answers: The army acts only for itself
The army is used as an instrument of the Lord
The army has no connection with the prophecy
challenge.explanation: The distant peoples are portrayed as weapons through which the Lord carries out judgment.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “the weapons of his indignation” reveal about the army’s power?

answers: They portray a public and organized summons to battle
They show that the army is hiding
challenge.explanation: These signs and calls emphasize the public gathering and preparation of the army.
challenge.q: Why are banners, voices, hands, and mountains mentioned together?

answers: From the mountains to the sea only
From a far country and the end of heaven toward Babylon
challenge.explanation: Verse 5 says they come “from a far country, from the end of heaven.”
challenge.q: From where does the army come according to the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Day of the LORD and the Terror of Defeat

easy.explanation: Verse 6 says, “the day of the Lord is at hand.”
easy.q: What is said to be at hand?

answers: Their hands become faint and their hearts melt
easy.explanation: Verse 7 says, “all hands shall be faint, and every man's heart shall melt.”
easy.q: What happens to people’s hands and hearts?

answers: The stars, the sun, and the moon
easy.explanation: Verse 10 mentions the stars, the sun, and the moon.
easy.q: Which heavenly lights are described as failing to shine?

answers: The nearness and fierce anger of the day of the LORD
medium.explanation: The passage presents the day of the LORD as a cruel day of wrath, destruction, and desolation.
medium.q: What causes the people to fear and become weak?

answers: Cry out in grief and fear
medium.explanation: “Howl ye” is a cry of mourning and distress because judgment is near.
medium.q: In the command “Howl ye,” what response is being required?

answers: Both describe the greatness of the day of judgment
Both show that Babylon is becoming stronger
medium.explanation: The darkened heavens and the ending of human pride both emphasize the severity of God’s judgment.
medium.q: How are the darkened heavenly lights related to the humbling of the wicked?

answers: The normal order of the world is shaken
challenge.explanation: The darkening of the heavenly lights reinforces the passage’s picture of cosmic upheaval.
challenge.q: What is the significance of the sun, moon, and stars no longer giving their light?

answers: The LORD brings down pride and shakes creation
challenge.explanation: The LORD causes “the arrogancy of the proud to cease” and shakes the heavens and the earth.
challenge.q: What connection does the passage make between human pride and heaven and earth?

answers: A movement from military preparation to celebration
A movement from human fear to the strengthening of the wicked
A movement from the announcement of the day of the LORD to fear, darkness, and cosmic shaking
challenge.explanation: The section progresses from the announcement of judgment to its effects on people, the heavens, and the earth.
challenge.q: Which development is described in verses 6–13?

paragraphs.title: The Army's Collapse and Brutal Destruction

answers: Every man to his own people and land
easy.explanation: Verse 14 says they turn to their own people and flee to their own land.
easy.q: Where do the people turn when the army is scattered?

easy.explanation: Verse 15 says, “Every one that is found shall be thrust through.”
easy.q: What happens to everyone who is found?

easy.explanation: Verse 17 says, “I will stir up the Medes against them.”
easy.q: Which people does the LORD stir up against Babylon?

answers: Those found are slain, while others flee to their own lands
The foreign armies surrender without a battle
medium.explanation: The passage describes some being thrust through while others flee to their own people and lands.
medium.q: What contrast is made between those found in the city and the fleeing armies?

answers: Scattered people without anyone gathering them
medium.explanation: The images describe people fleeing and being left without a gatherer.
medium.q: What does the image of a chased roe and a sheep that no man takes up suggest?

answers: To show that they cannot be bribed
To show that they are successful merchants
medium.explanation: Their lack of interest in silver and gold shows that wealth cannot buy them off.
medium.q: Why does the passage emphasize that the Medes do not regard silver or delight in gold?

answers: The army remains united and the city grows stronger
The army scatters, the city suffers, and the Medes advance without mercy
The city is abandoned without violence
challenge.explanation: The passage presents scattering, killing, plundering, and the advance of a relentless foreign force.
challenge.q: What does the sequence of these verses reveal about the severity of the defeat?

answers: The mention of children, houses, and wives
challenge.explanation: Verses 16 and 18 mention children, houses, wives, and the fruit of the womb.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the destruction affects more than soldiers?

answers: The people return to fight as one body
They scatter, flee, and become vulnerable
challenge.explanation: The images of the fleeing roe and un gathered sheep emphasize disorganization and vulnerability.
challenge.q: What is the result of the army’s loss of unity?

easy.explanation: Verse 19 compares Babylon’s overthrow to God’s overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah.
easy.q: To what is Babylon compared in its destruction?

answers: No, it will not be inhabited from generation to generation
easy.explanation: Verse 20 says it “shall never be inhabited.”
The passage lists wild beasts, owls, satyrs, dragons, and other creatures.

answers: From glory and excellence to desolation and ruins
From a small city to a great kingdom
From a desert to a trading city
medium.explanation: Babylon is called the glory of kingdoms, yet it will become desolate and ruined.
medium.q: What is the main contrast between Babylon’s former condition and its future condition?

answers: Animals that live in desolate places
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to wild creatures that will inhabit Babylon’s deserted ruins.
medium.q: In the phrase “wild beasts of the desert,” what kind of creatures are being described?

answers: Wild creatures occupy the houses and palaces instead of people
People build new homes throughout the city
medium.explanation: Animals and doleful creatures replace human inhabitants in the houses and palaces.
medium.q: How is the change from human life to desolation pictured?

answers: It emphasizes complete destruction and desolation
It teaches that Babylon will be saved
It describes trade between the cities
challenge.explanation: Sodom and Gomorrah represent a decisive and devastating overthrow.
challenge.q: Why does the comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah strengthen the description of Babylon’s fall?

answers: The cries and sounds of wild creatures
The sounds of a victorious army
challenge.explanation: The ruins are filled with cries of wild beasts and doleful creatures rather than human activity.
challenge.q: What replaces human voices in Babylon’s ruins?

answers: Babylon’s judgment will not be delayed for long
The city will immediately be rebuilt
challenge.explanation: The statement emphasizes that the appointed time of Babylon’s downfall is near and will not be extended.
challenge.q: What does the statement “her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged” mean?
